record.original_question: Does every triangular billiard, or more generally every polygonal billiard, contain at least one periodic orbit?

evidence.quote: We have the well known open question [62]: Open problem 5. Existence of periodic orbits: Do all triangular (or more generally polygonal) billiards contain at least one periodic orbit?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a polygon (a compact, simply connected planar region whose boundary is a finite union of line segments). The billiard flow on $P$ is the dynamical system describing a point particle moving with unit speed in straight lines inside $P$ and reflecting off the boundary $\partial P$ according to the law of equal angles (with reflections at vertices left undefined). A billiard trajectory is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections at smooth boundary points, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Question: Does every polygonal billiard table $P$ admit at least one periodic billiard trajectory? In particular, does every triangle $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ admit a periodic billiard trajectory?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is a well-known long-standing open question. Periodic orbits are known to exist for all rational polygons, all acute and right triangles, and (by computer-assisted work of R. E. Schwartz) for all triangles whose angles are at most 100 degrees. The general case for arbitrary obtuse triangles and arbitrary (irrational) polygons remains open.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Triangular Billiards II: 100 Degrees Worth of Periodic Trajectories
status_evidence.snippet: Schwartz gives a rigorous computer-assisted proof that every triangle with all angles at most 100 degrees has a periodic billiard path.
status_evidence.claim: Periodic orbits are established for triangles with all angles ≤ 100°, but the general case remains open.

status_evidence.title: Survey Lecture on Billiards (Schwartz, ICM)
status_evidence.snippet: Existence of periodic orbits in general polygonal billiards is described as a major open question, with partial results in the rational and nonobtuse cases.
status_evidence.claim: The existence of a periodic billiard orbit in every polygon (and every triangle) remains open in general.
